BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN)  -- Colombian officials are blaming the FARC guerrilla group for a car bombing late Sunday at a police station in Cali that killed two people and wounded at least 14. Residents check out a destroyed police building after a car bombing Sunday night in Cali, Colombia. It was the second bombing in Colombia attributed to the Marxist guerrilla group in less than a week. An explosion at a Blockbuster video rental store in an upscale Bogota neighborhood Tuesday killed two and wounded more than 20. The suspect in Sunday night's attack was killed in a shootout with police after the explosion, Cali Mayor Jorge Ivan Ospina said Monday, hours after convening a special security meeting in the middle of the night. "Although the explosive device only had moderate impact," Ospina said on the Cali government Web site, "we should not forget we are at war and the FARC has been committing terrorist acts in Bogota, Neiva, Cali and other cities in the country. That's why we cannot let our guard down, since they take advantage of Sundays and city centers, where control is more difficult." The explosion came just hours after the rebel group released four hostages in what many interpreted as a gesture to reach a peace accord with the government. Two officials also are slated to be released this week. FARC, which is the Spanish acronym for Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, is the largest and oldest revolutionary group in the nation and has been at war with the government for more than 40 years. According to Ospina, a blue and red Renault 12 Break pickup crashed into the police headquarters in Cali at 10:38 p.m. and then exploded. The driver tried to flee but was felled by two shots from uniformed police and died a few hours later at a hospital, the mayor said. The explosion caused damage in a two-block area, the Cali news Web site Semana.com said. Five of the 14 wounded were minors, Ospina said, citing emergency director Laureano Quintero. The injured are suffering from fractures and other wounds not considered life-threatening, he said. Cali's health minister, Alejandro Varela, said earlier 32 were wounded, including a pregnant woman who was in good condition. Others complained of hearing problems. The mayor's office said the previous higher tally could be a result of people not wounded in the bombing but seeking medical attention to receive government help. Three police were wounded, including a major with a broken arm and an officer who had to have three fingers amputated on his left hand, said the police chief, Gustavo Adolfo Ricaurte Tapia. The bombing caused a temporary power outage, which made security more difficult for officials, said the news Web site Burladero.com. It was the fourth bombing in Cali in less than 42 months, Semana.com said. The latest bombing took place about five blocks from the Palace of Justice, which was blasted by a car bomb in August, killing four and wounding 26. Police buildings were bombed in April 2007 and August 2006. The earlier blast killed five and wounded 17, Semana.com said. Security analysts say FARC has about 9,000 to 12,000 armed guerillas and several thousand supporters, mostly in rural areas. The guerrilla group was established in 1964 as the military wing of the Colombian Communist Party. The guerrillas operate mostly in Colombia but have carried out extortion, kidnappings and other activities in Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador, according to the Federation of American Scientists Intelligence Resource Program. Authorities said Sunday night's bomb contained 90 kilograms (198 pounds) of ammonium nitrate fertilizer and fuel, a commonly used explosive, Semana.com said. By comparison, the bomb that Timothy McVeigh used in the 1995 bombing in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, contained more than 2,800 kilos (6,200 pounds) of ammonium nitrate and diesel fuel.

**ATLANTA / CALI, Colombia —** At least five people were killed and more than 30 others injured early Thursday after a powerful car bomb exploded outside a major police station in the southwestern Colombian city of Cali, authorities said.

Officials have blamed the attack on dissident factions of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the leftist rebel group that largely demobilized following a historic 2016 peace treaty with the government. 

The blast occurred shortly after 7:00 a.m. local time in a densely populated neighborhood, targeting the station just as officers were changing shifts. The shockwave shattered windows for several blocks, destroyed nearby vehicles, and ripped through the facade of the multi-story precinct, sending a plume of thick smoke over Colombia’s third-largest city.

Emergency responders worked through twisted metal and concrete debris to rescue trapped survivors. Among the dead are three police officers and two civilians who were passing by the station at the time of the explosion, according to Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder.

"This was a cowardly and barbaric act of terror against our security forces and the people of Cali," Eder told reporters during a press conference near the smoking crater left by the vehicle. "We will not let violence intimidate this city. Those responsible will be brought to justice."

At least six of the injured remain in critical condition at local medical centers, hospital officials confirmed.

### A city on edge

Eyewitnesses described scenes of terror and confusion in the immediate aftermath of the detonation.

"The ground shook like an earthquake," said Maria Torres, 42, who runs a bakery two blocks from the station. "Then came the sound of twisted metal collapsing and people screaming for help. There was dust everywhere—you couldn’t see five feet in front of you."

Security forces quickly cordoned off the area, deploying bomb-sniffing dogs and anti-explosive units amid fears of secondary devices. Military helicopters were seen circling the city’s airspace as checkpoints were erected along major arterial roads leading out of Cali.

Colombian President Gustavo Petro condemned the attack and announced an emergency security council meeting with the nation’s top military brass. Petro vowed a swift military response against the perpetrator group, believed to be the *Estado Mayor Central* (EMC), the largest splinter faction of former FARC fighters who rejected the 2016 accord.

"The enemies of peace think they can force the state into retreat through terror," Petro said in a televised address. "They are mistaken. The full force of the public security forces will be deployed to dismantle these criminal structures."

### Escalating violence in Colombia's southwest

Thursday's bombing marks a sharp escalation in violence in the department of Valle del Cauca, of which Cali is the capital. The region has become a flashpoint for conflict in recent months as rival armed groups fight for control of lucrative drug trafficking routes leading to the Pacific coast.

Despite the 2016 peace deal that saw nearly 13,000 FARC fighters lay down their arms, intelligence reports estimate that several thousand dissident combatants remain active across Colombia. These groups have financed their operations through cocaine production, illegal mining, and extortion.

The U.S. State Department issued a security alert following the blast, advising American citizens to avoid the affected area and exercise heightened caution throughout Cali.

Authorities have offered a reward of 200 million Colombian pesos (approximately $50,000 USD) for information leading to the arrest of those who planned and carried out the bombing.

*CNN’s Stefano Pozzebon contributed to this report.*

# DEADLY CAR BOMB SHAKES CALI: FARC ATTACK LEAVES DEAD, DOZENS WOUNDED OUTSIDE COURTHOUSE

**CALI, Colombia** — A powerful car bomb detonated outside the Palace of Justice in downtown Cali late Sunday night, killing at least four people, injuring more than two dozen others, and tearing through several city blocks. Authorities have attributed the devastating attack to the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), marking a dramatic and violent resurgence of urban terrorism by the Marxist guerrilla group.

The blast occurred shortly past midnight, transforming a quiet city center into a war zone of shattered glass, twisted metal, and burning debris. Emergency responders rushed to the scene near the *Palacio de Justicia*, extracting victims from damaged buildings and transport vehicles. 

Military and police officials confirmed that the vehicle—a hijacked sedan packed with industrial-grade explosives—was parked directly adjacent to the judicial complex, which houses regional courts and prosecutors' offices.

### Mayor Ospina Condemns "Act of Pure Terror"

Speaking from the scene of the wreckage as rescue workers searched through the rubble, Cali Mayor Jorge Iván Ospina expressed deep outrage and called for unity in the face of violent intimidation.

"This is a criminal, terrorist act aimed directly at paralyzing our judicial institutions and striking fear into the hearts of our citizens," Mayor Ospina told reporters. "The perpetrators of this cowardice want to demonstrate power by slaughtering civilians and destroying public property, but Cali will not bow to terror."

Ospina immediately declared a state of high alert across the city, deploying additional military units to secure key infrastructure, government buildings, and transit hubs. 

"We are calling on the national government to bolster our intelligence capabilities," Ospina added. "We must find those responsible for placing this bomb and bring the intellectual authors of this massacre to justice. Our thoughts and full support are with the victims and their families tonight."

---

### A Devastating Payload: Comparing Cali to Oklahoma City

Defense experts and bomb technicians from the Colombian National Police reported that the car bomb contained approximately **100 kilograms (220 pounds)** of a high-grade explosive mixture, likely ANFO (ammonium nitrate and fuel oil) combined with commercial dynamite. 

While smaller in scale than some of the world's most infamous vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (VBIEDs), the payload produced immense localized destruction due to the narrow streets and reflective concrete walls of downtown Cali.

To put the blast into perspective, explosive experts drew comparisons to the **1995 Oklahoma City bombing** of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building—one of the deadliest VBIED attacks in modern history. 

* **The Oklahoma City Bombing:** Used a massive payload of approximately **2,200 kilograms (4,800 pounds)** of ANFO packed into a rental truck, resulting in the destruction of an entire nine-story building and 168 fatalities.
* **The Cali Bombing:** Contained roughly **1/22nd (under 5%)** of the explosive payload used in Oklahoma City. 

Despite carrying only a fraction of the yield used in the Oklahoma City attack, the Cali bomb’s shockwave was powerful enough to blow out reinforced windows five blocks away, cave in structural walls of neighboring commercial properties, and ignite multiple vehicle fires. Experts note that in dense urban corridors, even a payload modest by international terrorist standards can inflict catastrophic civilian casualties and severe structural shock.

---

### Context: A Desperate Response to Hostage Releases and Military Losses

The bombing comes at a critical juncture in Colombia’s decades-long internal conflict. Over the past year, FARC has suffered unprecedented strategic, political, and operational blows at the hands of President Álvaro Uribe’s U.S.-backed security forces.

Just months prior, the Colombian military executed **Operation Jaque**, a daring intelligence operation that successfully rescued 15 high-profile hostages without firing a shot—including former presidential candidate Íngrid Betancourt and three American defense contractors. That mission followed a series of unilateral and negotiated hostage releases earlier in the year, which had brought intense global media scrutiny to the rebel group’s treatment of captives held deep in the Amazon jungle.

Analyst suggest the attack in Cali is a deliberate strategy by FARC leadership to prove that despite high-profile military setbacks—including the deaths of top commanders Raúl Reyes and Manuel Marulanda earlier in the year—the guerrilla group retains the capability to strike deep within major urban centers. 

"FARC has been driven out of many rural strongholds and lost its top leadership," said Hugo Acero, a Bogotá-based security analyst. "When forced onto the defensive, they historically revert to urban terrorism to project strength and force the government back to the negotiating table on their terms."

---

### Background: FARC's Decades-Long War

Founded in 1964 as the armed wing of the Colombian Communist Party, the *Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia* (FARC) began as a rural peasant militia advocating for agrarian reform and Marxist political principles. 

Over the decades, however, the conflict evolved. During the 1980s and 1990s, FARC transformed into one of the wealthiest and best-equipped insurgent groups in the world, largely by funding its operations through taxation of the illegal cocaine trade, extortion, and mass kidnappings for ransom.

At its peak in the late 1990s, FARC boasted an estimated 16,000 to 18,000 fighters and controlled vast swaths of the Colombian countryside. However, hardline military offensives launched in the early 2000s under President Uribe severely degraded their numbers, pushing their remnants back into remote border regions and rainforests.

Sunday night’s attack in Cali serves as a grim reminder that despite significant military progress by the state, the insurgent group still poses a lethal threat to Colombia's urban populations.

As daybreak revealed the full extent of the ruin outside Cali's courtrooms, forensic teams continued to sweep the area for evidence, while city residents gathered to clear the glass from their streets—defiant, but shaken by the return of violence to their doorstep.

**By Stefano Pozzebon and CNN Staff**

A powerful car bomb detonated outside a police precinct in the southwestern Colombian city of Cali early Thursday morning, killing at least five people and injuring dozens more in what senior Colombian officials are calling a "cowardly terrorist attack" orchestrated by Marxist guerrilla factions.

The blast occurred at approximately 6:15 a.m. local time outside the police station in the densely populated *El Vallado* district, south-east of Cali's city center. The explosion shattered windows for blocks around, destroyed several adjacent residential buildings, and reduced a section of the police precinct’s outer compound to rubble. 

Speaking from the site of the wreckage, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder confirmed the current casualty toll and pointed the finger directly at leftist rebel groups operating in the neighboring departments of Cauca and Valle del Cauca.

"This is an atrocious, despicable act of violent intimidation against the people of Cali," Mayor Eder said during a press conference. "Initial intelligence overwhelmingly indicates that this attack was carried out by Marxist guerrillas seeking to retaliate against government pressure in the region. We will not be intimidated."

### Casualties and Medical Emergency

As of Thursday morning, authorities confirmed that five people—two police officers and three civilians, including a street vendor—were killed instantly in the blast. 

At least 38 others were rushed to nearby medical facilities, with emergency responders pulling several individuals from the smoking debris of collapsed facades. 

At the University Hospital of Valle (HUV), the city’s primary trauma center, medical personnel reported treating victims for severe blast trauma, shrapnel wounds, and third-degree burns.

"We have activated a state of maximum emergency across our trauma departments," said Dr. Luz Adriana Collazos, chief of emergency medicine at HUV, during a brief update to reporters. "At least nine patients are currently in critical condition in the intensive care unit, undergoing emergency surgeries for severe internal injuries and blunt force trauma. We are desperately calling on citizens to donate blood."

Civil defense workers and search-and-rescue teams, supported by sniffer dogs, continue to comb through the rubble of two multi-story homes directly across from the police station to ensure no residents remain trapped beneath the masonry.

### Authorities Target Leftist Insurgents

While no group has formally claimed responsibility for the morning attack, senior military and law enforcement sources told CNN that suspicion centers on two primary Marxist guerrilla organizations: the National Liberation Army (*Ejército de Liberación Nacional*, or ELN) and the *Estado Mayor Central* (EMC), the largest dissident faction of the former Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) that rejected the landmark 2016 peace accord.

Colombia’s Minister of Defense, Iván Velásquez, announced that he was deploying a special counter-terrorism unit to Cali and offered a reward of 200 million Colombian pesos (approx. $50,000 USD) for information leading to the arrest of the local commanders responsible.

"This tactic—using indiscriminate explosives in urban zones—bears the clear signature of guerrilla groups operating out of the rural sectors of Cauca," Velásquez said in Bogotá before boarding a flight to Cali. "They are attempting to transfer the theater of war from the countryside into our major urban centers."

President Gustavo Petro, Colombia's first leftist president, condemned the attack via social media, stating that the violence demonstrated the rebels' "lack of genuine desire for peace," referring to the ongoing, fragile peace talks his administration has attempted to maintain with various armed groups under his "Total Peace" policy.

### A Escalating Regional Security Crisis

Thursday’s bombing marks a dramatic escalation of violence in southwestern Colombia, a region that has become the epicenter of the country's renewed internal conflict over the past two years.

Cali, Colombia's third-largest city, sits strategically along key transit corridors connecting the coca-producing highlands of Cauca and Nariño to the Pacific port of Buenaventura—a vital hub for international drug smuggling. 

In recent months, security in the region has precipitously deteriorated:

*   **Failed Ceasefires:** Following the collapse of a localized ceasefire between the government and the EMC early this year, the military launched major offensives in the nearby Micay Canyon, a primary stronghold for drug trafficking and guerrilla finance. In response, insurgents have launched a wave of retaliatory attacks targeting security forces.
*   **Surge in Urban Attacks:** Over the past six months, neighboring towns in Cauca, such as Morales and Jamundí—just 15 miles south of Cali—have suffered repeated motor-bomb and drone attacks targeting police headquarters, killing over a dozen officers and civilians.
*   **Drones and Car Bombs:** Guerrilla factions have increasingly adopted asymmetric tactics, utilizing weaponized commercial drones and vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (VBIEDs) to hit soft targets, mirroring methods not seen in Colombia since the height of the armed conflict in the 1990s and early 2000s.

The blast in Cali comes at a particularly sensitive time for the city, which is preparing to host major international events and has been on high alert following intelligence warnings that armed groups intended to disrupt public order.

A citywide curfew has been implemented in Cali's eastern districts as military personnel and heavy armor deploy to secure critical infrastructure, government buildings, and entry points into the city.

*CNN's Stefano Pozzebon reported from Bogotá. Journalists in Cali contributed to this report.*
